article_title: Accelerated Middle Schools
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2008). WWC Intervention Report: Accelerated Middle Schools. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Accelerated middle schools share a common design: thematic cross-subject linking, experiential instruction, smaller classes, and added academic and social supports
description: Despite varying somewhat in instructional approach, the programs share several common design elements: "Classes are often linked thematically across multiple subjects"; instruction is "more experiential and 'hands on' than is typical in a traditional middle school"; classes are generally smaller than in traditional middle schools; and programs provide additional supports such as tutoring, attendance monitoring, counseling, and family outreach. This pattern describes the program-level configuration the three studied schools shared.
requirements: Additional instructional time in core academic subjects, obtained by offering relatively few electives
constraints: Programs vary somewhat in their approach to instruction; the pattern describes the three studied schools rather than all accelerated middle schools
target_learners: middle school students behind grade level
target_learning_goals: accelerated coverage of core academic curriculum
dropout prevention
examples: The three School Dropout Demonstration Assistance Program sites in Georgia, Michigan, and New Jersey
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2008). WWC Intervention Report: Accelerated Middle Schools. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/11

article_title: Flashlight360
citation: Flashlight360 program description. (2024). https://flashlight360.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/23505832409499-Device-Specifications
title: Deliver actionable language data so teachers can offer constructive feedback that accelerates language development
description: The article states that "By delivering actionable data, Flashlight360 supports teachers in offering constructive feedback, a proven approach to accelerating language development." The principle is that progress-monitoring tools should give teachers actionable data on specific language areas so feedback can be focused and meaningful for both teachers and students working toward proficiency.
requirements: Scoring and feedback across defined language areas (five speaking areas, three writing areas) so feedback can be targeted
target_learning_goals: Speaking and writing language proficiency
examples: Flashlight360 delivers scoring and feedback across five areas of speaking and three areas of writing to guide teacher and student efforts toward proficiency.
key_sources: Flashlight360 program description. (2024). https://flashlight360.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/23505832409499-Device-Specifications

article_title: Guide to Measuring Implementation: The 3Us – Usability, Usefulness, Utilization
citation: Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Andrew Gothro, Ryan Ruggiero. (2023). Guide to Measuring Implementation: The 3Us – Usability, Usefulness, Utilization. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/guide-to-measuring-implementation-the-3us-usability-usefulness-utilization
title: Use implementation measurement results to guide what implementing organizations do next
description: The guide treats measurement as actionable: beyond describing when and how to measure the 3Us, it addresses "what implementing organizations can do with the results." The principle is that usability, usefulness, and utilization data should feed decisions about refining and scaling a solution, not sit as a compliance artifact.

constraints: The guide describes this principle for solutions during development and early implementation
target_learning_goals: data-informed improvement of educational solutions
examples: The guide's stated purpose includes telling implementing organizations what they can do with measurement results

article_title: How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools?
citation: Max, Jeffrey; Tuttle, Christina; Gleason, Philip; McCallum, Diana; Gill, Brian. (2019). How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools? Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Policymakers evaluating school choice should account for its effects on students who remain in traditional public schools, not only on participants
description: The brief argues that school choice policy analysis must look beyond participants. As it states, "Policymakers considering school choice need to understand how it affects students who attend schools of choice, but they should also account for its effect on students who remain in traditional public schools." The brief frames this broader accounting as essential for policymakers weighing charter schools and vouchers.
requirements: Evidence on choice effects must cover both participants and students remaining in traditional public schools
target_learners: students in traditional public schools affected by charter schools and voucher programs
target_learning_goals: student achievement in traditional public schools under school choice policies
examples: The brief summarizes key findings on how charter schools and private school vouchers affect achievement in traditional public schools and discusses implications for policymakers

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Early Education Essentials: Testing Measurement Validity of an Organizational Conditions and Practices Tool for Early Childhood Education Settings. (2018). https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Use organizational-conditions survey data to give ECE leaders actionable information about supports for practitioner effectiveness
description: The article positions organizational-conditions measurement as a leadership tool: the survey "has the potential to provide leaders and practitioners with actionable data about organizational supports that enable ECE practitioners to be more effective in their daily work with children and families." Programs should thus measure organizational conditions alongside classroom-level quality metrics to guide improvement.
requirements: Reliable, site-sensitive survey administration with teacher and parent perceptions
constraints: The overview states potential; the associations with quality metrics held for some, but not all, measured conditions
target_learning_goals: identifying organizational supports that improve daily work with children and families
examples: Site-level essential scores were related to teacher–child interaction scores and student attendance in 81 ECE sites

article_title: Teaching Adolescents to Become Learners
citation: Farrington, C.A., Roderick, M., Allensworth, E., Nagaoka, J., Keyes, T.S., Johnson, D.W., & Beechum, N.O. (2012). Teaching adolescents to become learners. The role of noncognitive factors in shaping school performance: A critical literature review. Chicago: University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Evaluate noncognitive-factor evidence for actionability: malleability, classroom context, and teacher strategies
description: The review argues identification alone is insufficient for practice: "Validating the claim that schools would get high payoffs from working on noncognitive factors requires an evaluation of whether the supporting evidence is 'actionable' for practitioners." Evidence is actionable only when the factor is shown to be malleable, shown to be affected by classroom context, and accompanied by research-based strategies teachers can use within regular instruction. Practitioners would ideally also track change in the targeted factor.
requirements: Randomized experimental designs that show interventions change both the factor and grades, plus clarity about mechanisms rather than leaving a black box
constraints: Much existing research is correlational, and mechanisms of change in experiments often cannot be observed
target_learners: Adolescent students in middle grades, high school, and transition to college
target_learning_goals: Course grades and development of noncognitive factors
examples: For each of the five categories the review asks how the factor relates to grades, whether it is malleable, what role classroom context plays, whether actionable strategies exist, and whether changing it would narrow gender or race/ethnicity gaps

article_title: School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomialmodel in a program evaluation context
citation: Soland, J. & Thum, Y.M. (2019). School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomial model in a program evaluation context. The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper.
title: Accountability systems should account for the seasonality of achievement data, since ignoring summer loss changes which schools are identified as effective
description: The article argues that because school effectiveness estimates differ depending on whether fall-to-spring or spring-to-spring growth is used, accountability models should not ignore summer learning loss. The authors state that "a broader policy conversation is likely needed about the extent to which schools should be responsible for how learning changes during the summer months," and show that no correlation they produced reached the .90 threshold at which rank orderings would agree.
requirements: Requires assessment data collected at multiple points within the year (e.g., fall and spring) and a growth model that can parameterize within-year growth, since states testing only once per year cannot model within-year growth
constraints: The authors note the CP findings are sensitive to parameterization choices such as the centering grade, so the model cannot definitively identify effective and ineffective schools
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair estimation of school contributions to student growth for accountability determinations
examples: The authors compared school-level fall-to-spring and spring-to-spring growth estimates from CP models fit to five years of MAP Growth data and found all correlations below the .90 threshold
key_sources: Soland, J. & Thum, Y.M. (2019). School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomial model in a program evaluation context. The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/school-effectiveness-summer-loss-and-federal-accountability-applying-the-compound-polynomialmodel-in-a-program-evaluation-context/

article_title: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models
citation: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models. (2019). NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Account school accountability models for summer learning loss
description: School accountability models should incorporate seasonal learning patterns rather than assuming uniform growth across the calendar year. The brief's rationale is that "ignoring summer loss can impact which schools are identified as low performers", meaning models that omit summer loss risk misclassifying schools. The principle directs accountability designers to use growth estimates that separate school-year learning from summer learning before labeling schools.
requirements: Assessment data collected across seasons, including fall and spring (or summer-adjacent) administrations, so summer loss can be estimated separately from school-year growth
constraints: The supplied text does not print the specific modeling procedure the brief recommends
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate school accountability classifications
examples: The brief examines how estimates of school effectiveness change when seasonality is taken into account
key_sources: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models. (2019). NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/reconciling-long-term-education-policy-goals-with-short-term-school-accountability-models/

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Provide adult learners a large bank of easily accessible practice resources in multiple formats
description: The brief's third principle calls for many opportunities for practice and repetition, since adult learners need increased practice to activate brain plasticity and growth. Digital products should store many resource types (documents, PDFs, videos, sound files) because audio, video, and games increase engagement by being less threatening and more fun than reading text. Resources must also be easy to access, because perceived support correlates with persistence in online learning and access struggles are major roadblocks for adults with limited time and digital confidence.
requirements: Resources of many types and in learners' languages must be available
Access must be clear and simple, avoiding difficult navigation and multiple logins
constraints: LMSs and other storage options often suffer usability problems such as difficult navigation and the need for multiple logins, which can make resources effectively unavailable to adults with low digital confidence
target_learning_goals: practice and repetition
persistence in online learning
examples: Washington State adult educators found that having good resources in both English and Spanish was imperative for their largely ELL participants; LMSs, YouTube channels, and wikis are cited ways to centralize resources
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Disseminate actionable findings early, plan scale pathways, and govern data with FAIR principles and privacy-enhancing technologies
description: Teams should translate R&D findings into practical, actionable insights for stakeholders and industry developers, and consider scale pathways such as commercialization or licensing early so development aligns with dissemination needs. Data work requires "the technical, operational, and legal infrastructure required to protect student and educator privacy," going beyond traditional compliance to address challenges from emerging technologies like generative AI, with policies on data provenance, algorithmic transparency, and continuous monitoring. Data management should be grounded in the FAIR principles to lower access barriers, prevent redundant efforts, and support transparency and replicability.
requirements: Clear policies on data provenance, algorithmic transparency, and continuous monitoring; FAIR-grounded data management
constraints: Traditional compliance expectations are insufficient for ethical, safety, and privacy challenges introduced by emerging technologies like generative AI
target_learners: education R&D teams, learning providers, industry developers
target_learning_goals: responsible scaling and open sharing of breakthrough solutions
examples: The note names commercialization and licensing to established providers as example pathways to scale
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

title: Acknowledge students for demonstrating expected behaviors through positive attention, praise, and rewards, rated moderate evidence
description: Recommendation 3 directs teachers to acknowledge expected behavior using behavior-specific praise, positive attention, and rewards. Table I.1 rates this recommendation moderate, and the panel views Recommendations 1–3 together as the foundation for supporting expected behavior.

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Build a learning culture with three components — acceptance and trust, accountability, and appreciation — so students take academic risks and support each other's learning
description: The brief states that a supportive learning culture "includes three primary components: acceptance and promotion of trust and academic risk-taking, accountability for one's own and other's learning, and appreciation of each person's unique gifts and perspectives." In such a culture, English learners trust that teacher and peers value mistakes as sources of new learning, take risks with language and ideas, and can access affordances such as anchor charts, task directions, and language supports like formulaic expressions and images.
requirements: Teachers demonstrate and cultivate trust and respect, provide models for risk-taking and mutual support, create a physical environment that enables exploration, and establish and practice norms for listening and responding to each other's ideas.
target_learners: All students (ELs and non-ELs) in a classroom community
target_learning_goals: Open sharing of partial or emergent ideas and effective formative assessment
examples: Using learning goals and success criteria, every member can give descriptive, actionable feedback, which the brief says levels the playing field between peers and lets even emergent learners assume a leadership role.

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The access–success paradox and its resolution through embedded support infrastructure
description: The report names the access–success paradox: the assumption "that expanding access to more students who do not typically participate in advanced coursework must necessarily be accompanied by declining success, particularly for the students with the most to gain from expanded opportunity." Policy attention focuses on removing entry barriers while neglecting what enables enrolled students to succeed. OUSD's experience provides the report's answer: open-access dual enrollment can achieve equitable outcomes, but only when vague commitments to student support are transformed into concrete, systematic infrastructure—an embedded adult, continuous monitoring, proactive response to struggles, and structured communication between systems.
requirements: Intentional, resourced support infrastructure embedded in course structure rather than offered as an external add-on service
constraints: The report offers OUSD as an existence proof, "not a prescription to be replicated exactly"; support of this kind is described as not very affordable
target_learners: High school students historically underserved in advanced coursework, including Black and Hispanic students, students with disabilities, and English Learners
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation and success in college coursework while in high school
examples: OUSD pairs open eligibility (no GPA requirements, no prerequisites, no teacher recommendations) with the point person model, achieving scale of nearly 70 sections per semester with an 83 percent average pass rate.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: ACEs Aware Initiative
description: The ACEs Aware Initiative, driven by California's first surgeon general, focuses on screening children, youth, and adults for adverse childhood experiences, training medical providers, and improving public awareness. The guide reports "over 500,000 people have already been screened, and the ACEs Aware Initiative has the ambitious goal of reducing ACEs by half within one generation." ACEs are 10 categories of adversities in three domains experienced by age 18, linked to toxic stress and long-term health issues. Schools participate by building trauma-informed, healing-centered environments within local networks of care.
requirements: A whole school approach led by a principal and a cross-department leadership team, with staff attending to their own positive and adverse experiences before students'
constraints: One-time COVID-19 relief funds such as ESSER-1 and GEER must be used by September 2022
target_learners: Children, youth, and adults screened for ACEs; students from low-income backgrounds, English Learners, students experiencing homelessness or in foster care named for relief funds
target_learning_goals: Reducing toxic stress and creating trauma-informed school environments that support learning and well-being
examples: The guide recommends developing a leadership team, connecting one-time and ongoing funds (LEA BOP, SMAA, EPSDT Medi-Cal services), and educating personnel about PACEs science with time for buy-in
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science
citation: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three-component framework of academic language: content-domain vocabulary, general academic vocabulary, and discipline-specific sentence structures
description: The report defines academic language as school language valued by teachers, texts, and tests, structurally and lexically different from everyday spoken English. It divides academic language into three components: "(1) vocabulary related to the academic content domain; (2) general academic vocabulary related to the words used within the discipline to tie ideas together; and (3) sentence structures required by the content discipline." It illustrates the components with a butterfly life-cycle unit and echoes the bricks-and-mortar analogy distinguishing content-specific vocabulary from general academic terms like therefore and because.
requirements: Instruction must treat all three components so English learners can succeed in content-area instruction
constraints: The framework is illustrated with elementary science examples (butterfly life cycle, pendulum, rocks)
target_learners: English learners in U.S. K-8 schools
target_learning_goals: Academic language development in content areas
Content understanding in science
examples: In an elementary butterfly unit, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis are content vocabulary; grow, change, transform are general academic vocabulary; first, then, next, last structure sequencing sentences
key_sources: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580362

article_title: A Step Forward or a Step Back? State Accountability in the Waiver Era
citation: Daria Hall. (2013). A Step Forward or a Step Back? State Accountability in the Waiver Era. The Education Trust. http://www.edtrust.org
title: Good accountability systems pair ambitious, achievable expectations with mechanisms that prompt meaningful action
description: The report argues that well-designed accountability systems rest on two priorities: expectations and action. Good systems set "improvement and gap-closing expectations that are both ambitious" and achievable, and they go beyond evaluation to "celebrating and rewarding schools that exceed expectations and acting when schools repeatedly fall short." The report uses these two priorities as the criteria against which it judges every state waiver plan, organizing ten diagnostic questions for educators, advocates, and policymakers.
requirements: Goals must apply to students overall and to each student group, including low-income students, students of color, English-language learners, and students with disabilities.
Performance against goals must be incorporated into school rating or grading systems so that meeting goals actually matters.
constraints: The report states accountability systems themselves do not raise achievement: only the hard work of teachers and students can do that; systems are tools that must be assessed with multiple years of data.
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly low-income students, students of color, English-language learners, and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Raising achievement and closing achievement and graduation-rate gaps for all student groups
examples: Minnesota makes the percentage of students overall and in student groups meeting cut-the-gap-in-half goals a meaningful component of its Multiple Measure Rating.
Massachusetts bases a district's performance rating on the designation of its lowest performing school, making the district only as strong as its weakest link.
key_sources: Daria Hall. (2013). A Step Forward or a Step Back? State Accountability in the Waiver Era. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED543222

article_title: Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars
citation: Pascal Riachi, Sofie Kamber, Stella Brogna, Andrew Gloster, Rafael Wampfler. (2026). Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786
title: Embodied simulated-patient training application for ACT-oriented psychotherapy practice with spoken dialogue
description: A Unity application enabling interactive psychotherapy practice through real-time spoken dialogue with an embodied virtual patient. It uses a dual-LLM architecture: GPT-4o generates patient responses from structured prompts, while GPT-4o mini evaluates each therapist utterance for ACT-consistency. Speech is processed with Azure Cognitive Services, and responses are rendered through text-to-speech synchronized with facial and body animations. The authors state it is "designed exclusively for training and research purposes".
requirements: Voice input and transcription of therapist utterances
Structured patient profiles and training scenarios to condition patient behavior
constraints: Designed exclusively for training and research purposes, not real patient encounters
target_learning_goals: ACT intervention skills
Therapeutic fidelity to ACT processes
examples: Two psychologists each interacted with the system for approximately 90 minutes across scenarios including suicidality, resistance, and dramatic escalation.
key_sources: Pascal Riachi, Sofie Kamber, Stella Brogna, Andrew Gloster, Rafael Wampfler. (2026). Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786

article_title: Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery
citation: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org
title: Treat accessibility attenuation as a first-class part of a security mechanism, with its cost stated rather than assumed away
description: The principle holds that when a security mechanism adds sensory load, accommodation should be incorporated directly into the same adaptation law rather than as a separate opt-out system bolted on afterward, and the security cost of accommodation should be quantified and made visible. The article operationalises this with an accommodation coefficient applied multiplicatively to adapted intensity, so attenuation reduces the visual footprint without exempting the candidate from ordinary integrity evaluation.
requirements: Diversion intensity must already be a dynamic, per-candidate quantity rather than a fixed platform-wide setting, so that accommodation can act on the same adaptation law.
constraints: Attenuation does not preserve capture degradation; at full accommodation the unsynchronised-channel fidelity guarantee fails, so the institution must plan replacement assurance such as reallocated evidence weights or supervised delivery.
target_learners: candidates with registered visual-processing accommodations, photosensitivity, or attention-related conditions
target_learning_goals: equitable access to high-stakes digital assessment without unintended equity burden
examples: The model sets an accommodation coefficient ai in [0,1] through the institution's existing accessibility-declaration process, where ai = 1 fully suppresses the diversion field regardless of behavioural evidence.
key_sources: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03531

article_title: Governing academic integrity: Ensuring the authenticity of higher thinking in the era of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Hamish Coates, Gwilym Croucher, Angel Calderon. (2025). Governing Academic Integrity: Ensuring the Authenticity of Higher Thinking in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09639-7
title: Academic integrity indicator framework: 130 items organised under eight dimensions of academic integrity
description: A governance-level indicator framework for the integrity of student assessment, in which "130 specific items were detailed and organised under eight dimensions of academic integrity". The dimensions, shown in Table 1 with item pool sizes and sample items, span designing assessment and governance arrangements, developing assessment resources, training, assessment implementation, analysis and reporting of assessment data, evaluation, and improvement. The parameterisation is deliberately general to yield governance-relevant insights across disciplines and levels, and items are sampled from dimension-specific pools onto a 100-point reporting metric.
requirements: Data collected across an institution, preferably at department, discipline or course level, to furnish insight beyond the institution level
A governance need for such intelligence and interpretative intelligence to hand
constraints: The pilot quantitative data was not designed to be representative or generalisable either educationally or statistically
Further validation requires collecting more quantitative data and psychometric validation
target_learning_goals: integrity of student assessment and qualifications
examples: Sample items include whether the institution's top-most board receives updates on assessment processes, and what percentage of assessment is designed to have robust academic integrity qualities

article_title: Characterizing LLM-Based Family Education through the Lens of Activity Theory: A Scoping Review of the HCI Literature
citation: Lan Luo, Yuqi Liang, Jie Cai, Anqi Wang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Muzhi Zhou, Chun Yu, and Pan Hui. (2026). Characterizing LLM-Based Family Education through the Lens of Activity Theory: A Scoping Review of the HCI Literature. arXiv:2609.28886. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28886
title: Activity theory operationalized through AODM as a framework for analyzing LLM-based family education
description: The review uses activity theory, which takes the activity system as the unit of analysis and examines how people pursue an object through a mediating tool within a socially organized setting. It is operationalized through the Activity-Oriented Design Method (AODM), which the review says "provides an operational bridge by translating the components and relations of an activity system into research questions and representations for empirical analysis." The framework relates subjects, objects, tools, community, rules, and division of labor to explain how LLM capabilities become organized through family participation.
requirements: Studies must be analyzable in terms of a focal activity configuration with identifiable subjects, object, tools, rules, community, and division of labor
constraints: The review treats a study as family education only when a family relationship meaningfully shapes how an educational interaction involving an LLM-based system is organized

description: ACLIME is a conceptual framework structuring human-agent interaction in immersive learning media. citation: Chinomso Nwagboso & Sunday Atuba. (2026). Academic erasure: the disappearance of complexity under AI-supported writing. Teaching in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/13562517.2026.2707601
title: Academic erasure: loss of depth, voice, and engagement in AI-shaped student writing operating through compliance
description: Academic erasure is the study's central concept: "the disappearance of depth, voice, and engagement in student writing shaped by AI-driven norms". Unlike marginalisation, which excludes students who fail to meet standards, erasure operates through compliance — the student may meet all standards yet produce epistemically vacuous work. The article characterises it by three features: superficial structure without depth, fluency without complexity, and generic tone with weak positioning, and frames it as structurally enabled by institutions that reward fluency and output.
requirements: Assessment cultures that reward fluency, presentation, and output over argumentation and intellectual risk, which the article says create conditions in which AI use is rational

critical thinking
epistemic agency

title: Consensus working definition of active learning versus traditional lecturing
description: The article establishes an operational definition of active learning built from written definitions collected from 338 audience members at biology departmental seminars, then coded into a consensus statement: "Active learning engages students in the process of learning through activities and/or discussion in class, as opposed to passively listening to an expert." It emphasizes higher-order thinking and often involves group work. Traditional lecturing is defined, following Bligh, as continuous exposition by the teacher, with student activity limited to note-taking and occasional unprompted questions. requirements: Studies admitted to the comparison had total class time devoted to each approach not differing by more than 30 min/wk

course failure rates
examples: Interventions coded under the definition included occasional group problem-solving, in-class worksheets or tutorials, personal response systems with or without peer instruction, problem-based learning, and studio or workshop course designs.

description: The article frames STEM learning as an active process of integrating abstract knowledge against intuitive preconceptions, requiring struggle, metacognitive processing, embodiment, and social support. description: The article describes academic mindset as "the beliefs, attitudes, or ways of perceiving oneself in relation to learning and intellectual work that support academic performance" (Farrington et al., 2012). The study operationalizes these on the PERTS instrument at the classroom level, extending individual mindset theory to group/classroom data. examples: The PERTS 15-item survey was administered district-wide in April 2016 to measure the four constructs

description: The acculturation complexity model (Tadmor and Tetlock, 2006) links varying levels of engagement with two cultures to cognitive skill development. citation: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003
title: Access deficit hypothesis: mathematical difficulties arise from impaired access to numerical magnitude from symbols
description: The access deficit hypothesis (attributed to Rousselle & Noël, 2007) states that "mathematical difficulties originate from impairments in accessing numerical meaning, i.e. their quantity, from symbols rather than from difficulties in processing numerosity per se." It contrasts with the defective number module hypothesis, which posits a deficit in representing quantities itself. The article tests the two by comparing performance on symbolic versus non-symbolic tasks, and its first-grade findings — symbolic deficits with intact non-symbolic performance — favour the access deficit account.
requirements: Distinguishing the hypotheses requires comparing performance on numerical tasks with and without a symbolic processing requirement
constraints: Evidence remains behavioural; the authors note neural-level abnormalities in non-symbolic processing are not precluded
General factors such as intellectual ability and working memory were not directly administered

target_learning_goals: accessing numerical magnitude meaning from symbolic numbers

title: ACE-C: a group-administered digital executive function assessment battery for classrooms
description: The Adaptive Cognitive Evaluation Classroom (ACE-C) is a digital assessment battery of nine tasks measuring executive functions such as attention, working memory, and multitasking, administered on iPads to groups of students in school settings. Tasks were "developed from cognitive assessments commonly used in lab-based settings and modified to include adaptive algorithms, motivational trial-by-trial and end-of-task feedback, and a user-friendly interface." Psychometric staircase adaptive algorithms let students perform the same tasks across time points without floor or ceiling effects. This study used its continuous performance task (CPT), adapted from the TOVA, to derive a sustained attention component score.
requirements: Administered on iPads in group school sessions with trained researcher facilitators present; a basic response time task is included at the start of each session for processing-speed correction
constraints: The authors note tablet-based direct assessments are limited in assessing complex behaviors integrating interpersonal dynamics or social and emotional factors
target_learning_goals: measurement of sustained attention and other executive functions in naturalistic school contexts
examples: In this study, 725 students completed the ACE-C CPT in group sessions of 7 to 83 students lasting approximately 50 minutes in classrooms, libraries, cafeterias, and gymnasiums
key_sources: Gallen, C. L., Schaerlaeken, S., Younger, J. W., Project iLEAD Consortium, Anguera, J. A., & Gazzaley, A. (2023). Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children. Scientific Reports 13, 2673. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-29427-w

article_title: Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts
citation: Gerry Stahl, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9189-4
title: Activity Theory as a multi-level framework for analyzing systemic contexts of CSCL practices
description: The editorial presents Timmis's use of Activity Theory as a framework for "understanding the complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, and as a result how new technological innovations and knowledge-creation practices can be appropriated and sustained." It references micro, meso, and macro units of analysis—individuals' actions, small-group discourse, and community practices—and expands the theory toward dialogicality and communicative action, treating small-group interaction as the intermediate level bridging micro and macro.
requirements: Studying how micro-level processes can be transformed into persistent macro-level knowledge-construction practices
constraints: An illustrative multi-level analysis of UK college students revealed contradictions, e.g. course assessments opposing individual grades to collaborative work, which militate against sustainability of the educational innovation
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
appropriation and institutionalization of CSCL practices
examples: Timmis's multi-level analysis of college students in the UK showing assessment contradictions against sustainability
key_sources: Gerry Stahl, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9189-4

article_title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
citation: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0
title: Knowledge-building pedagogy model with initial acculturation to collaborative culture before introducing Knowledge Forum
description: A design pattern emergent from failed starts in the Hong Kong teacher network: students are first acculturated to a collaborative culture before the Knowledge Forum tool is introduced. This reverses the typical Canadian approach where "Knowledge Forum is usually included at the start of knowledge building." The pattern addresses the tendency of new teachers and students to focus on the tool rather than collaborative knowledge construction.
requirements: Teachers must understand that students can work together to build knowledge before the platform is introduced
constraints: Emergent from the Hong Kong socio-cultural context where examination pressure and teacher-directed norms prevail
target_learners: Grade 5-12 students in Hong Kong classrooms
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge building
Community knowledge creation
examples: Unsuccessful starts with Knowledge Forum led to the teacher-researcher design of a pedagogy model including an initial acculturation phase

article_title: Does Burnout Affect Academic Achievement? A Meta-Analysis of over 100,000 Students
citation: Madigan, D. J. & Curran, T. (2020). Does burnout affect academic achievement? A meta-analysis of over 100,000 students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09533-1
title: Academic burnout as a three-symptom syndrome (exhaustion, cynicism, reduced efficacy)
description: The article defines academic burnout as "a multidimensional syndrome of exhaustion from studying, cynicism directed to one's study, and reduced efficacy in relation to academic work", adapting the original occupational burnout construct to students on the grounds that student activities can be considered "work". The framework treats the three symptoms as separable but related predictors, each hypothesised to undermine achievement via reduced effort, disengagement, and absenteeism. The meta-analysis tests and confirms negative relationships for the total score and each symptom separately.
requirements: Measurement via validated instruments capturing the three symptoms, such as the SBI or MBI-SS
constraints: The construct was examined only in secondary and tertiary education; the authors note there is currently no understanding of its effects in primary education
target_learning_goals: sustaining effort and engagement in academic study
protecting academic achievement from ill-being
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's burnout instrument (SBI or MBI variants) and estimated separate pooled correlations for total burnout and each of the three symptoms
key_sources: Madigan, D. J. & Curran, T. (2020). Does burnout affect academic achievement? A meta-analysis of over 100,000 students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09533-1

article_title: Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings
citation: Lucciarini, E., Carr, A., Bressoud, N., Boniwell, I., Audrin, C., Gay, P., & Burel, N. (2025). Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10033-3
title: ACTIONS framework: seven categories for classifying positive psychology interventions
description: The ACTIONS framework (Boniwell, 2017) organises PPIs into seven categories: Activity, Calming, Thinking, Identity, Optimising, Nourishing, and Social. The review states that "Through systematic analysis, Boniwell developed seven distinct categories that better reflected the diversity of the PPIs as detailed in Table 2." Each category carries key elements, e.g. Activity covers movement and sport, Calming covers mindfulness and breathing, Identity covers character strengths and values, and Social covers positive relationships and prosocial behaviour. The review uses ACTIONS to structure consideration of the 64 selected interventions for future implementation.
requirements: Derived from a review of 12 meta-analyses encompassing over 60 distinct PPIs
target_learning_goals: wellbeing
psychosocial skills
examples: The review evaluated its 64 selected PPIs using the ACTIONS framework to support implementation decisions

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Account for both sampling and imputation error when analyzing plausible values, using weights and Rubin's rules
description: The article recommends that secondary analysts of PVs weight student observations to restore population representativeness, repeat each analysis separately across all PVs (usually 5 to 10), and aggregate results using Rubin's rules with replicate-weight variance estimation. Without these steps, analysts 'risk underestimating the amount of uncertainty in their findings', which can lead to overstated claims.
requirements: Use the representation weights provided in publicly available datasets; perform each analysis separately per PV and aggregate with Rubin's rules; include replicate weights for sampling uncertainty
constraints: PVs cannot simply be averaged to produce an overall score for a student, a common misconception the article identifies
target_learners: educational researchers conducting secondary analysis of large-scale assessment data
target_learning_goals: valid population-level statistical inference from PV data
examples: TIMSS and PIRLS use Jackknife Repeated Replication methods and PISA uses Fay-adjusted Balanced Repeated Replication to produce replicate weights included in public datasets

article_title: Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework
citation: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9
title: Integrative action-model framework with six stages of motivated action
description: The article proposes an integrative framework for six major motivation theories grounded in the Heckhausen and Heckhausen action model. The basic model is "deliberately parsimonious, consisting of six stages of action: the situation, the self, the goal, the action, the outcome, and the consequences." Motivational constructs from expectancy-value, social cognitive, self-determination, interest, achievement goal, and attribution theory are mapped onto these stages, revealing "differences and to a lesser extent commonalities." The model builds on the Rubicon model of action phases and treats motivated behavior as arising from person-environment interaction.
requirements: The framework requires mapping each theory's constructs onto the six action stages to compare theories against a common background
constraints: The article states the model is intentionally parsimonious and that the situation, though the overarching context, is depicted by only one box
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting the direction, initiation, intensity, and persistence of learning behaviors
examples: The article maps situated expectancy-value theory, social cognitive theory, self-determination theory, interest theory, and the 3x2 achievement goal model onto the six-stage model in separate figures
key_sources: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9

article_title: Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom
citation: Jarodzka, H., Skuballa, I., & Gruber, H. (2020). Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09565-7
title: Actor-perspective by setting taxonomy for classroom eye-tracking research
description: The article organizes eye-tracking research in education along two axes: the actor perspective studied (teacher vs. learner vs. teacher-learner interaction) and a continuum from laboratory to real-life settings. Figure 1 clusters existing research and the Special Issue articles into these boxes, showing that classic eye-tracking research sits in the learner-laboratory corner while interaction studies in real classrooms are the newest and scarcest. The authors state that existing research beyond the classic learner-laboratory box "is extremely scarce."
requirements: Eye-tracking methodology, optionally enriched with verbal protocols, to capture what actors saw and how they interpreted it
constraints: Apart from classic learner-on-material laboratory research, existing research in the other boxes is extremely scarce
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of visual perception in teaching and learning
examples: Figure 1 places the six Special Issue empirical articles into the learner, teacher, and interaction boxes along the lab-to-real-life continuum

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model
citation: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6
title: When investigating presentation-pace effects during learning, take learners' prior knowledge into account
description: This principle follows from the article's experimental findings: the TBRS model assisted investigation of information presentation pace effects during learning only "as long as prior knowledge is taken into account". Researchers and designers studying time-paced instruction should therefore measure or control learners' prior knowledge, since it conditions whether pace effects can be characterized with the model.
requirements: Learners' prior knowledge must be measured or accounted for when studying or designing for presentation-pace effects.
target_learning_goals: optimizing information presentation pace for learning
examples: In the article's two experiments, hypotheses from the TBRS model were tested and the model's usefulness for investigating pace effects was shown conditional on prior knowledge.

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Achievement goal complex: fused reason-goal construct operative in self-regulation
description: The goal complex concept captures the idea that energization and direction become enmeshed during self-regulation: when energization prompts a goal, they 'fuse together to create a third reason-goal combined construct that is represented in memory and operative in self-regulation.' Structurally it takes the form 'Try to X in order to Y' or 'Try to X because Y.' The concept is highly flexible, broadly applicable to competence-based and non-competence-based reasons, and ecologically valid in capturing idiographic daily self-regulation.
requirements: Both the energization source and the goal must be identified, since the same goal can be fused with different energization sources and the same energization with different goals
constraints: The billiard ball metaphor, in which energization is left behind after prompting the goal, does not adequately capture how energization and direction work together in actual daily self-regulation
target_learning_goals: competence-relevant self-regulation and goal pursuit
examples: Example complexes as printed: 'Try to do well compared to others in order to experience the satisfaction of competitive success' versus 'in order to avoid losing my scholarship and go further into debt'
key_sources: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7

article_title: Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7
title: Academic resilience as a contextually embedded adaptive capacity, distinguished from lower-intensity academic buoyancy
description: The review frames academic resilience as students' capacity to sustain or recover adaptive academic motivation, engagement, learning behavior, and performance under substantial academic adversity, emphasizing "exposure to academic adversity and adaptive functioning in response to that adversity." Academic buoyancy is distinguished as a lower-intensity form covering everyday setbacks such as poor grades and negative feedback. Drawing on resilience theory, ecological systems, and motivational perspectives, the framework treats resilience as an adaptive process situated within learning environments rather than a purely individual disposition, and evaluates competing unidimensional, multidimensional, hierarchical, and bifactor measurement operationalizations without assuming one in advance.
requirements: Instruments must explicitly anchor items, instructions, or validation purposes to academic adversity, schoolwork, learning, grades, examinations, or school contexts
constraints: The review notes a general factor may emerge from homogeneous self-report items or restrictive analytic models rather than a genuinely broad construct; dimensionality evidence was interpreted alongside item content and scoring purpose
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: adaptive academic functioning under academic stressors, setbacks, failure, or threat
examples: Table 1 summarizes frequently used measures including the ARS-30, ABS, ARRS, SRS, SRQ, MRS, and domain-specific scales for pharmacy, English learning, programming, and nursing education
key_sources: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7

article_title: Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7
title: Corpus of 46 studies of academic resilience and buoyancy instrument validation (48 study–instrument combinations, 51 records)
description: The review's analytic dataset comprised quantitative studies published between 2000 and February 2026, identified through five databases following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The final dataset included "46 unique studies, 48 unique study–instrument combinations, and 51 study–sample–instrument records," all restricted to academic- or education-specific instruments; no domain-general resilience measure was retained. Studies were double coded with discrepancies resolved through deliberation, and covered dimensionality, internal consistency, and construct validity evidence across educational levels and geographic regions.
requirements: Studies had to report extractable psychometric evidence such as model-fit indices, reliability coefficients, or validity correlations with sufficient statistical information
constraints: Formal meta-analytic tests of measurement invariance were not conducted because item-level covariance matrices or comparable parameter estimates were unavailable for most studies
target_learners: students in formal education (primary, secondary, higher education)
target_learning_goals: psychometric evaluation of academic resilience measurement
examples: The search yielded 2,325 records across five databases, of which 46 studies were included after screening

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Academic Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ): a multidimensional self-report instrument measuring nine academic emotions across class-, learning-, and test-related situations
description: The AEQ is a multidimensional self-report instrument developed from the authors' qualitative data, measuring "students' enjoyment, hope, pride, relief, anger, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, and boredom." It uses multiple items per emotion to represent affective, cognitive, physiological, and motivational components, with separate scales for class-related, learning-related, and test-related emotions, and trait, course-related, and state versions. Short eight-item versions and an English-language version (average reliability α = .86) are also reported.
requirements: Domain-specific items constructed from exploratory student reports and test anxiety measurement standards
Separate scales for the three academic situations (class, learning, test)
constraints: Relief is measured for test emotions only; boredom for learning-related and class-related emotions only
target_learning_goals: measuring academic emotions as predictors of self-regulated learning and achievement
examples: Trait scale reliabilities reported in Table 3 range up to α = .94 (test anxiety, hopelessness)

article_title: A scoping review on word-reading resilience in literacy: Evaluating empirical evidence for protective factors
citation: Appels, S., van Viersen, S., van Erp, S., Hornstra, L., & de Bree, E. (2024). A scoping review on word-reading resilience in literacy: Evaluating empirical evidence for protective factors. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101969. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101969
title: A framework and operationalization of study designs and statistical approaches for studying academic resilience in literacy
description: The review provides a framework for studying academic resilience that distinguishes promotive, protective, and skill-enhancing factors in atypical literacy development. It aims to "provide a framework and operationalize study designs and statistical approaches for studying academic resilience", giving researchers concrete design and analysis tools for resilience research in word-level reading.
requirements: Studies must include samples of children with a detectable (risk of) word-level reading difficulty and at least one relevant literacy outcome measure
target_learners: 6- to 16-year-old children with (a risk of) word-level reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Word-level literacy outcomes in the face of reading difficulty
examples: The review applied the framework to 22 empirical studies of compensation in literacy development, evaluating whether their designs could distinguish factor types

article_title: Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students’ emotions, well-being, and health
citation: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089
title: Six-group model of achievement emotion regulation strategies derived from control-value theory
description: The article proposes a theoretical model in which university students regulate achievement emotions using six strategy groups. As the authors state, the model "is derived from the control-value theory of achievement emotions (Pekrun, 2006) and Harley et al.'s (2019) model of emotion regulation in achievement settings" and "considers six groups of strategies: situation selection, social support, reappraisal, expression,suppression,andcompetencedevelopment." Strategies target different elements of reciprocal feedback loops between emotions, appraisals, situations, and competence.
requirements: Measures must be context- and emotion-specific, since the model holds that emotion regulation is context-specific and emotion-specific
constraints: The model was developed and tested with university students in Germany and England
target_learning_goals: regulating achievement emotions such as enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom during studying, attending class, and taking tests

article_title: Context-related changes in academic self concept development: On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects
citation: Becker, Michael; Neumann, Marko. (2016). Context-related changes in academic self concept development. On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects. Learning and instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.003
title: When interpreting students' academic self-concept, account for the achievement level of the classroom context
description: Because classroom ability composition shapes academic self-concept, educators and researchers interpreting a student's ASC should consider the achievement level of the surrounding classroom. The article shows that "contextual characteristics play an important role in driving changes in self-perception" and that equally able students report different ASCs depending on classroom achievement. It also cautions that contextual effects can change across school transitions, so the current context matters most.
requirements: Knowledge of the achievement composition of the student's current classroom
constraints: The elementary-school context's influence was no longer discernible after one year in secondary school, so prior-context information has limited lasting value
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of academic self-concept
supporting healthy academic self-concept
examples: The longitudinal study followed fourth graders through the elementary-to-secondary transition, tracking how BFLPEs from each context affected their ASCs over time.

article_title: Relations between classroom disciplinary problems and student motivation: Achievement as a potential mediator?
citation: Arens, A. Katrin; Morin, Alexandre J. S.; Watermann, Rainer. (2015). Relations between classroom disciplinary problems and student motivation. Achievement as a potential mediator? Learning and instruction 39. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.07.001
title: Achievement as a mediator of the relation between classroom disciplinary problems and student motivation
description: The article proposes and tests an account in which classroom disciplinary problems relate to student motivation both directly and indirectly through achievement. The title frames the question as "Achievement as a potential mediator?" and the results support verbal achievement as the pathway: "in most cases, the relation between classroom disciplinary problems and motivation constructs was mediated by verbal achievement." This positions reduced achievement as a key mechanism linking disorderly classrooms to lower competence self-perceptions, higher test anxiety, and lower engagement.
requirements: Requires measures of disciplinary problems, verbal achievement, and multiple motivation facets collected at the student and classroom levels
constraints: Mediation held in most but not all cases; direct relations with motivation remained
target_learners: Primary school students in language classes
target_learning_goals: Maintaining student motivation under classroom disciplinary problems
Understanding the role of achievement in motivation formation
examples: The study tested mediation of discipline-problem effects on competence self-perceptions, test anxiety, and engagement via verbal achievement

article_title: The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings: Feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement
citation: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715
title: Account for learners' self-enhancement and self-verification motives when designing feedback
description: Because "feedback preference is motivated", feedback design in educational settings should recognize that learners' acceptance of feedback depends on competing motives: the desire for positive evaluation and the desire for subjectively accurate information. The article shows that when self-enhancement motivation is increased, learners may prefer positive feedback "regardless of its perceived accuracy", so accuracy-focused feedback may be discounted under such motivation.
requirements: Awareness of learners' current self-enhancement motivation and their established self-perception in the relevant domain.
constraints: Evidence concerns feedback on social abilities under laboratory conditions; the positivity preference was mainly observed for participants with positive self-perception.
target_learning_goals: effective feedback processing and uptake
examples: In the laboratory studies, participants chose between one positive and one negative evaluation of their social abilities under varying self-enhancement motivation.

article_title: A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task.
citation: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000
title: Action-control theory of motivational beliefs (agency beliefs, means-ends beliefs, control expectancy)
description: Action-control theory (Skinner et al., 1988) conceptualizes control-related beliefs that mediate motivated action in the school domain. It integrates perceived-control theories including locus of control, causal attributions, learned helplessness, and self-efficacy. The article states these beliefs "form a belief system with a sequential distinction among agent, means and ends," comprising agency beliefs (perceived ability to utilize means such as effort and ability), means-ends beliefs (beliefs about which means produce desired outcomes, including internal means like effort and ability and external ones like luck), and control expectancy (perceived control over actions toward desired outcomes). The study uses these constructs as profile indicators.
requirements: Measurement of agency beliefs for ability and effort, control expectancy, and means-ends beliefs for ability and luck as distinct but related belief constructs
constraints: The article notes means-ends belief for ability can be adaptive or maladaptive depending on its conjunction with other beliefs such as perceived own ability or control expectancy
target_learners: secondary school students, including students with special educational needs
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and effort exertion in learning tasks
examples: The study measured agency beliefs for ability (e.g., "I have suf ﬁcient ability to succeed at school") and effort, control expectancy, and means-ends beliefs for ability and luck with three-item 7-point Likert scales

article_title: Attitude as a determinant in spelling efficiency in immediate and delayed recall.
citation: Arps, G. P. (1917). Attitude as a determinant in spelling efficiency in immediate and delayed recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Arps+attitude+spelling+efficiency
title: Accidental spatial-temporal contiguity acts as a temporary recall crutch that aids immediate reproduction but interferes with permanent retention
description: The article's explanatory account of why the two procedures reverse between immediate and delayed recall. Under orderly assignment, words acquire "a unique, temporary, and accidental contiguity" that functions during immediate reproduction but fades almost wholly by delayed recall, and whose total final effect is negative because it interferes with clear phonetic connections of a word's literal elements. The article illustrates this with a pupil who, when March followed missed in the learned order, said "I was thinking of 'smell.'"
requirements: Recall situations in real life lack the spatial and temporal references present in orderly school assignments, so the crutch cannot transfer
constraints: Derived from observation of a single learner in initial spelling work, within the limits of that study
target_learners: primary-grade children in initial spelling work
target_learning_goals: permanent retention and accurate reproduction of spelling words
examples: When March in the reproductive order followed missed, the pupil was confused, stating "I was thinking of 'smell.'"

article_title: Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties.
citation: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832
title: Active View of Reading (AVR): reading comprehension depends on active self-regulation skills alongside word recognition and linguistic comprehension, with vocabulary as a bridging process
description: The Active View of Reading (Duke & Cartwright, 2021) extends the Simple View of Reading by adding self-regulation to the reading domains. As the article states, "The AVR model posits that for students to successfully comprehend text, in addition to having adequate skills in the reading domains, successful readers need to employ active self-regulation skills, which includes motivation, strategy use, and EF." Within AVR, vocabulary bridges word recognition and linguistic comprehension rather than belonging solely to linguistic comprehension. The article uses AVR to justify including executive functioning and attention measures and to interpret why the attention-stronger profile benefited more from intervention.
requirements: Adequate skills in the reading domains (word recognition and linguistic comprehension) plus active self-regulation skills including motivation, strategy use, and executive functioning
constraints: The article applies AVR to elementary students with reading difficulties in Grades 4–5; the framework is cited from Duke and Cartwright (2021) rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: Elementary school students, including students with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension

citation: Putwain, D. W., Wood, P., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000671
title: Academic buoyancy as adaptive response to minor academic adversity
description: Academic buoyancy is "the ability to respond adaptively to the everyday challenges, setbacks, and pressures experienced by students during their studies", such as poor performance, dips in confidence, negative feedback, and test demands. It is distinguished from academic resilience, which concerns major adversities. The construct is theorized to buffer the detrimental impact of negative emotions on achievement; this study tested that buffering role with a mathematics-specific buoyancy measure in primary students.
requirements: Domain-specific measurement is recommended; the article notes relations with achievement are stronger when analyzed in a domain-specific fashion
constraints: Buoyancy's benefit for performance diminished at higher anxiety levels; it did not protect performance against anxiety at high levels
target_learning_goals: coping with everyday academic setbacks
mathematics achievement
examples: Buoyancy was measured at T3 with a four-item mathematics-specific adaptation of the Academic Buoyancy Scale

A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Smartphone-Based Well-Being Training in Public School System Employees During the COVID-19 Pandemic. title: Awareness, Connection, Insight, and Purpose (ACIP) training-based model of well-being
description: The ACIP model, proposed by Dahl and colleagues, holds that well-being rests on four trainable pillars: "awareness, connection, insight, and purpose (ACIP)". Awareness comprises attention and meta-awareness skills; connection emphasizes prosocial dispositions such as gratitude and kindness; insight targets clarity about the nature of one's identity and experience; and purpose aims to clarify values and apply them in daily life. The model claims these pillar skills "demonstrate plasticity" and that this plasticity "can be harnessed through intentional practice," specifically meditation training. The Healthy Minds Program app and this trial's hypotheses were constructed around this framework.
requirements: Skills in each pillar are strengthened through repeated, intentional meditation practice over time
constraints: The authors did not preregister predicted improvements in purpose for the four-week intervention, assuming changes in purpose occur over a longer timescale

target_learning_goals: Reduced psychological distress and strengthened well-being skills (attention, prosocial dispositions, defusion, purpose)
examples: The four-week Healthy Minds Program Foundations course delivered one week of content per ACIP pillar to school system employees

article_title: Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning
citation: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z
title: Accuracy–applicability trade-off account of generalization breadth
description: The article explains generalization breadth via a trade-off: narrower generalization is "more likely to be accurate" but applies to fewer new objects, while broader generalization applies to more cases but is less likely to be accurate; the learner seeks a "sweet spot". The paper proposes that expecting high variability in the application context shifts this trade-off toward broader generalization, so learners "cast a wider net" by attributing the outcome to a broader range of stimuli. This is the mechanism account the three experiments were designed to test.
requirements: An anticipated application context whose variability the learner can represent, so the trade-off point can shift before generalization occurs
constraints: Derived from the notion of the trade-off (ref. 18) and supported here behaviorally; the article notes the task cannot separate perceptual non-discrimination from expecting the same outcome
target_learners: adult online experiment participants (Mechanical Turk, Prolific, Israeli panel)
target_learning_goals: broad vs narrow generalization of learned stimulus–outcome contingencies to novel, similar stimuli
examples: In Experiment 1, participants told to expect samples from labs across the world predicted "pathogenic" for more of the smaller, previously unseen rings than participants told to expect samples from the same lab
