article_title: Longitudinal markers of cognitive procedural learning in fronto-striatal circuits and putative effects of a BDNF plasticity-related variant
citation: Lena S. Geiger, Torsten Wüstenberg, Zhenxiang Zang, Mirjam Melzer, Stephanie H. Witt, Marcella Rietschel, Markus M. Nöthen, Stefan Herms, Franziska Degenhardt, Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg & Carolin Moessnang. (2024). Longitudinal markers of cognitive procedural learning in fronto-striatal circuits and putative effects of a BDNF plasticity-related variant. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00282-2
title: Adaptive Control of Thought (ACT) three-stage model of procedural learning
description: The article adopts the ACT model, a behavioral account of procedural memory in which procedural learning occurs in three main stages: an initial encoding drawing heavily on cognitive demands with rapid performance improvement, a reactivation-and-modification stage with a gradually reached performance plateau, and a transition to longer-term retention with stable, automatized performance at reduced cognitive demand. The study uses this framework to motivate hypotheses about exponential behavioral learning curves and declining fronto-striatal activation, citing reduced brain activation as the neural signature of automatization.
requirements: Repeated training across multiple sessions so that the staged transition from controlled to automatized performance can be observed longitudinally.
constraints: The article notes that most imaging evidence for reduced activation comes from pre-post designs, which do not allow modeling based on the law of practice assumption.
target_learners: healthy young adults performing verbal working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: procedural learning and automatization of cognitive skills
examples: The study tested ACT-derived hypotheses with a modified Sternberg task across five fMRI sessions, fitting linear and exponential learning curves to behavior and to activation in 246 Brainnetome parcels.

citation: Ockelmann, J., Scherpiet, S., Stropahl, M. & Giroud, N. (2025). Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00369-4
title: ActivEar: a gamified, personalized mobile auditory-cognitive training app on the CogniFit platform
description: ActivEar is a mobile ACT application used as the experimental intervention, delivered via the CogniFit research platform with training contents "drawn from the ActivEar mobile application." After installation, the CogniFit cognitive assessment battery (CAB™) established baseline performance, which "informed the automated synthesis of a personalized training plan" prioritizing each participant's lowest-scoring abilities and updating after every training unit. Units comprised two training tasks and a concluding assessment task, with gamification elements such as adaptive difficulty and reward systems.
requirements: Daily training of at least 20 minutes, five days a week, over four weeks, logged via the CogniFit platform.
constraints: Sensory aspects were integrated into broader cognitive tasks rather than trained separately.
target_learners: older adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss, with or without hearing aids
target_learning_goals: working memory, phonological short-term memory, selective attention, divided attention, and speech-in-noise comprehension
examples: Experimental-group participants completed four weeks of home-based ActivEar training, with activity automatically logged by the application.

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: When genetic confounding cannot be controlled, researchers must state it as a limitation and hedge environmental causal claims to avoid parent blaming
description: The article's renewed call for reporting standards: when none of the genetic-control options are possible, researchers should "clearly mention the possible genetic confounding as a limitation", and be cautious with environmental causal statements, which "could lead to unnecessary parent blaming" or wasted interventions. This principle exists because prior reviews' calls failed by not offering actionable correlational design solutions to researchers outside behavior genetics, so researchers published confounded work rather than doing nothing.
requirements: Awareness of the passive gene–environment correlation mechanism and of the available control designs (genetically sensitive, PGS, Familial Control Method)
constraints: Observational genetically sensitive designs cannot establish causality or its absence; they can only strongly infer it above typical observational studies
target_learners: behavioral and educational researchers; journal editors and reviewers
target_learning_goals: improving causal inference standards in research on parenting and home environments
examples: The article notes reviews have asked editors and reviewers "to insist that manuscripts adhere to these standards", yet conference talks and press coverage still present uncontrolled causal claims

citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Academic Resistance Model: cognitive, emotional, and intentional attitudes toward organizational change complement TAM
description: The Academic Resistance Model (ARM), introduced by Piderit (2000), accounts for cognitive, emotional, and intentional attitudes about an organizational change, complementing the Technology Acceptance Model's focus on usefulness and ease of use. The article cites Rienties (2014) as an illustration: educators cognitively appreciated the usefulness of a new student evaluation system yet felt strong negative emotional attitudes and resisted the change due to anxiety and mistrust. ARM is offered as a lens for understanding educators' resistance to AI-powered systems.
requirements: Applying the model requires attending to emotional and intentional attitudes toward change, not only cognitive perceptions of usefulness.
target_learners: Educators facing organizational adoption of new education technology
target_learning_goals: Understanding and addressing educator resistance to education technology adoption
examples: Rienties (2014) found educators who cognitively appreciated a new student evaluation system's usefulness still resisted it due to anxiety and mistrust.

citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9

APTA belongs to guiding systems providing peer interaction support, which the article further distinguishes, citing Magnisalis et al., from group formation and domain-specific support. Guiding systems must handle ambiguity in assessment, modeling, and support phases.

A model of ideal collaborative interactions
A support mechanism that intervenes when weaknesses are perceived

Domain learning through collaboration

citation: Vassileva, J., McCalla, G. I., & Greer, J. E. (2015). From Small Seeds Grow Fruitful Trees: How the PHelpS Peer Help System Stimulated a Diverse and Innovative Research Agenda over 15 Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0073-9
title: Active user modelling paradigm: user model as a context-based computation, not a knowledge structure
description: The active user modelling paradigm arose when the authors observed that in their distributed MAGALE architecture each user held up to 20 fragmented models stored across many agents, so that in a real sense the user model ceased to be an object. It views user modelling as a process, "a computation (function) over a space of four major dimensions: subjects, objects, purposes and resources", where the subject does the modelling, the object is modelled, the purpose is the adaptation served, and the resources contribute information. It shifts focus from representation issues to the process of collecting, interpreting and utilising user data for a particular purpose, making it a procedural rather than declarative approach.
requirements: A purpose for which the model is being created, plus defined subject, object and contributing resources for each modelling activity
Ability to interpret multi-modal information from multiple heterogeneous sources and integrate it into a user model of appropriate granularity
constraints: When user models are fragmented in a decentralized architecture there is no single user model at all, only the subset of user characteristics important to the task at hand
target_learners: Learners and workers in distributed help and learning systems
target_learning_goals: Context-appropriate helper recommendation and adaptation
examples: A multi-agent recommender system for investment portfolio management built on a library of purpose-based user modelling processes combined at run time depending on context and resource availability

citation: B. Barros & M. F. Verdejo (2015). Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:113–123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0063-y
title: Activity Theory-based declarative methodology for defining collaborative learning scenarios (dialogue, task, outcome template)
description: The project's first core contribution is a methodology based on Activity Theory that provides declarative mechanisms for specifying collaborative scenarios. An intermediate language creates a generic template with three elements (dialogue, task, and outcome) used to build a scenario-instance from a taxonomy of values; a framework then interprets the instance to launch an interactive online learning environment. The authors situate this approach within the later development of collaborative scripts and collaborative learning flow patterns. It was implemented in DEGREE and re-implemented in subsequent system versions.

target_learning_goals: collaborative learning process design and analysis
examples: The template approach evolved as a research field within CSCL, scripts (Dillenbourg 2002), and collaborative learning flow patterns (CLFPs), and lay within the scope of educational modelling languages such as IMS and PALO

citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Activity Theory framing of tool, task, user, and community of practice
description: The article borrows Activity Theory as an orientation and vocabulary for authoring tool usability, because it "stresses the mediating role of tools (artifacts) and their usage rules in collective human activity". It frames usability as the interaction between users, tools, rules, and tasks, and asks whether a tool and its rules of use afford a particular task for a particular class of users, including socio-cognitive complexity of the community of practice and division of labor.

article_title: Active Grade Estimator on Short Answer Assessment
citation: Mohammad Iqbal, Tsamara Rana Nugraha and Hsing-Kuo Pao. (2024). Active Grade Estimator on Short Answer Assessment. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-5651820/v1
title: Active Grade Estimator (AGE): a pool-based active learning model for automated short answer grading with two-stage sampling, assessment voting, and grading estimation modules
description: AGE is a pool-based active learning model for automated grading systems (AGSs) that integrates LLMs and regression models. It consists of three major modules: "two-stage sampling, assessment voting, and grading estimation modules". The two-stage query first selects the most contextually similar student answer via cosine similarity, then rewrites it via LLM canonicalization and simplification before teacher annotation. A voting mechanism based on minimum error grading estimation reduces annotation bias from multiple teachers, and a regression model estimates grades for remaining ungraded answers.
requirements: Requires a pool set of ungraded student answers, a set of answer keys, and teacher(s) to grade selected answers iteratively until a stopping condition is met.
constraints: The composition function must apply canonical construction before simplification, as the reverse order may lose information.
target_learners: students in online courses with short-answer assessments
target_learning_goals: automated grading of short answers
examples: The model was demonstrated on the UNT and SciC datasets with different grading tasks (regression and classification).

citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Adaptive collaborative learning support (ACLS): intelligent technologies that assess collaborative interaction and deliver tailored pedagogical interventions
description: ACLS is defined as the intersection of CSCL and AIED research: "ACLS involves the use of intelligent technologies to improve student collaboration and learning by assessing the current state of the interaction and providing a tailored pedagogical intervention". Unlike typical intelligent tutoring, its goals are to improve collaboration between two or more students rather than support an individual learner. Support can focus on group formation, domain knowledge, or peer interaction, produced with natural language processing, machine learning, and user modelling techniques.
requirements: Assessment of the current state of the interaction to tailor interventions
constraints: Differs from individual intelligent tutoring because its goal is improving collaboration between students, not individual learning
target_learners: students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: domain learning and collaboration skills during computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The APTA system provides peer tutors with reflective prompts, using an integrated cognitive model and machine classifier to diagnose domain errors and ineffective tutoring approaches

article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Taxonomy of ACLS support dimensions: timing, psychological realm, mode, locus, target, and type of support
description: The article organizes ACLS research around dimensions drawn from prior taxonomies: "identify dimensions such as the timing of support (whether it is provided immediately or with some delay during the collab- oration, or before or after the collaboration), the psychological realm of support (cognitive, social, metacognitive, motivational, affective)". Further dimensions are the mode of support (explicit or implicit), the locus of support (direct or indirect), the target of support (group formation, domain knowledge, peer interaction, social skill), and the type of support (guiding, challenging reflection, mirroring). The paper uses these dimensions to structure its research agenda and to diagnose the Dystopian system's uncoordinated support.

description: The article distinguishes the two central issues directionally: "Accountability is the reverse of explainability. title: The access hypothesis of OER benefits
description: The access hypothesis, named by Grimaldi, Basu Mallick, Waters, and Baraniuk (2019), is an explanatory mechanism for OER effects: "OER benefits learning by providing access to critical course materials, and therefore predicts that OER should only benefit students who would not otherwise have access to the materials." The commentary presents it as a current direction toward stronger theorization of OER research.

constraints: Predicts benefits only for students who would not otherwise have access to the materials

target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes such as final grades and success metrics through affordable access to course materials

citation: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Academic controversy: a five-step cooperative group controversy procedure
description: Academic controversy is a cooperative learning technique in which "cooperative student groups of four members" investigate an issue, split into pro/con diads, and work toward a "best reasoned judgment" under instructor monitoring. The lesson proceeds through five steps: prepare a position, present and advocate it, engage in open discussion and critique, reverse perspectives, and synthesize a joint position. The article operationalized this procedure in eight macroeconomics lessons.
requirements: Groups of four students split into pro/con pairs, with an instructor overseeing and monitoring the controversy
Rules for criticizing ideas without criticizing people during open discussion
constraints: Examined here only in post-secondary macroeconomics at one community college
target_learning_goals: economic reasoning and understanding of macroeconomics content
critical thinking through considering multiple perspectives
examples: In the study, lesson packs were distributed on Tuesdays and group controversy sessions held in class on Thursdays, approximately every two weeks, across eight lessons in spring 2010

title: Academic controversy lesson pack for macroeconomics
description: The lesson pack is the instructional artifact used in the experimental treatment, based on the Johnson and Johnson procedure. "It contained an issue page consisting of the question to be investigated and the steps to conduct the controversy," a rules page, background with key terms and potential resources, pages for research, position, and consensus notes, and rubrics for scoring. Students prepared positions outside class and turned in the completed pack with a group synthesis report.
requirements: Students find credible resources and prepare their assigned position outside of classroom time
Scoring via rubrics developed from Harvard University guidelines (Goodrich, 1997)
target_learning_goals: preparing and advocating evidence-based positions
synthesizing opposing arguments into a joint position
examples: Each student quad also wrote a report explaining the synthesis and supporting evidence, and students were assessed individually on controversy topics via class examinations

title: Teachers should take an active role in and out of class when using videos and 3D animations to remedy misconceptions
description: The article concludes that the teacher's active contribution supported the success of remedying misconceptions with videos and 3D animations. In class, "The prominent roles were acting as guidance to the students, monitoring students , and focusing on the frequently observed misconceptions"; outside class, the teacher administered projects, followed activities, and evaluated homework step by step. requirements: Teacher guidance such as suggesting slowing down, replaying, rewind or forwarding during video and animation tasks
constraints: In the homework condition students could not ask questions about the concepts, though this did not affect the difference in conceptual change between groups
target_learners: 10th-grade vocational high school students in the computer department
target_learning_goals: Remedying misconceptions about basic computer system concepts
examples: The classroom teacher introduced videos and animations with short notices, provided presentations and question-and-answer sessions, and sometimes let students work individually or together

title: Under any teaching approach, teachers should accustom students to pose metacognitive questions to themselves and answer them with relevant reasons
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that, since no single teaching approach guarantees higher MLTA, teachers should accustom students to pose metacognitive questions to themselves and then attempt to answer the questions or solve the problems together with relevant reasons. examples: In the study, MTL students were awakened to control and assess their thinking process through posed questions, answered with relevant reasons, connecting new knowledge with previous knowledge

title: Eight-week active listening training program organized around listening types
description: The experimental intervention was a weekly two-hour course for eight weeks (16 hours total) in which students studied informative texts, narrative texts, a poem and a video, each tied to a listening type (discriminant, listening for information, empathetic, critical, aesthetic) and "performing activities in accordance with the process steps of active listening method". Sessions progressed from defining active listening and listening types to applying each type to a curriculum-appropriate text.
requirements: Texts appropriate to students' levels, selected from books suitable for fourth and fifth grade levels and approved materials; audiovisual tools including a TRT School short film
constraints: Delivered within Turkish lesson hours (40-minute lessons, two per week); control group studied the same materials via traditional listening exercises such as note taking and teacher questions

examples: Session 3 used the narrative text "Atatürk's High Sense of Humanity" for discriminant listening; Session 8 used the short film "The First Flying Man" for aesthetic listening

article_title: An RCT of a CBT Intervention for Emerging Adults with ADHD Attending College: Functional Outcomes
citation: Laura D. Eddy, Arthur D. Anastopoulos, Melissa R. Dvorsky, Paul J. Silvia, Jeffrey D. Labban & Joshua M. Langberg (2021). An RCT of a CBT Intervention for Emerging Adults with ADHD Attending College: Functional Outcomes. Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2020.1867989
title: ACCESS: a two-semester CBT and mentoring program for college students with ADHD
description: ACCESS (Accessing Campus Connections and Empowering Student Success) is a cognitive-behavioral treatment program delivered over two academic semesters for emerging adults with ADHD attending college. The first-semester active phase includes "eight weekly group sessions (90 minutes each)" covering ADHD psychoeducation, behavioral strategies, and adaptive thinking, plus up to 10 weekly 30-minute individual mentoring sessions supporting implementation. The second-semester maintenance phase fades support to one group session and up to six mentoring sessions. Groups of four to six students used a discussion-based format with handouts and guest speakers from campus support services.
requirements: Delivery requires trained group leaders and mentors with weekly supervision by licensed doctoral-level clinical psychologists and a detailed treatment manual
constraints: Evaluated at two large public four-year universities; authors note findings may not generalize to other postsecondary settings or students with markedly lower intellectual abilities
target_learners: college students with ADHD (emerging adults, ages 18–30)
target_learning_goals: ADHD knowledge, behavioral strategies addressing executive functioning deficits, adaptive thinking skills, study skills, time management, daily life functioning
examples: In the RCT, 83.2% of the immediate treatment group attended at least 6 group sessions and 85.7% attended a majority of mentoring sessions; fidelity ratings were 96.4% and 95.6% for reviewed group and mentoring sessions.

article_title: Accelerated Reader: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See. (2015). Accelerated Reader Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.gl-assessment.co.uk/products/new-group-reading-test/test-detail
title: Accelerated Reader: web-based reading management and monitoring programme
description: Accelerated Reader (AR) is a commercial web-based reading programme by Renaissance Learning that screens pupils with the STAR test, matches books to reading level and interest using the ATOS readability formula, and motivates independent reading through computerised quizzes, AR points and TOPS reports. The report describes it as "a whole-group reading management and monitoring programme that aims to foster the habit of independent reading". In the trial it was delivered for about 20 weeks as a catch-up intervention for weak readers in Year 7.

Regular subscription to the Renaissance Learning website for STAR tests and quizzes
Computers or tablets with internet connection
constraints: ATOS measures only readability level and does not take into account literary merit, thematic construction, quality and complexity of ideas or maturity of the content
The intervention involves no teaching at all
target_learners: Year 7 pupils below secure Level 4 in KS2 English
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Independent reading habit
Reading motivation
examples: Schools ran 40 minutes of daily independent reading, used library space for reading and quizzes, and purchased tablets and books with trial funding

article_title: Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course
citation: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166
title: Select modeling tasks by accessibility, independence and activity principles
description: For forming representations of modeling methodology in secondary schools, the article holds that "accessibility, independence and activity the methodical principles are considered to be the main principles of selection of tasks". Task selection should satisfy accessibility and clearness, since modeling is an intersubject method spanning mathematics, computer science and the researched area. Tasks should also be rich enough to show modeling's key property: approximate description of reality and checking model adequacy.
requirements: Tasks must satisfy the accessibility and clearness principle
Tasks should reflect the recurrence and variability of the modeling methodology, not only text tasks from algebra
constraints: Satisfying accessibility and clearness is described as the main difficulty of task selection
target_learning_goals: formation of representations of modeling methodology
examples: The article gives example tasks: proposing essential assumptions for a tent-production planning task, calculating train speed from wheel knocks, and drawing a bicycle in a graphics editor

title: Shift ESP classroom practice from passive lecture to active group learning to increase target-language exposure
description: For EFL contexts where learners have little contact with native speakers, the article recommends moving away from teacher-centred translation: "the focus of language teaching should be placed on changi ng the classroom practice fr om the traditional passive lecture to more active group learning so that learners can be more easily exposed to target language use." The principle rests on the study's finding that the interactive, feedback-rich task-based condition outperformed individual translation work, and it extends to implications for materials development and teacher training.
requirements: Learner-learner interaction during tasks so students can discuss vocabulary and monitor their language
constraints: Recommended for EFL contexts with limited native-speaker contact, such as Iran
target_learners: University ESP students in EFL contexts
target_learning_goals: Technical vocabulary acquisition
Communicative competence
examples: The experimental classes replaced text translation with pair and group tasks, giving students peer feedback the traditional group never received

Item discrimination index of at least 0.30
constraints: Designed to measure knowledge and skills gained during the 12-week Teaching Practice course only

examples: Scored 1-0 per item and assessed over 100 points before and after the application, with the mean of both scores forming actual performance

citation: Agâh Tuğrul KORUCU, Hasan ÇAKIR. (2018). The Effect of Dynamic Web Technologies on Student Academic Achievement in Problem-Based Collaborative Learning Environment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://www.mojet.net

constraints: Used as both pre-test and post-test in this study with pre-service ICT teachers

examples: Scoring assigned 1 for correct and 0 for wrong answers, and item discrimination power and reliability were determined after application

citation: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://ber.journals.pu.edu.pk

self-direction
applied problem solving and transfer of information and skills

Collaboration among researcher, teacher and administrator roles
Objective data in the form of learner language and classroom interaction
constraints: The article notes action research is an emerging framework in educational research with several similar competing models

communication
self-efficacy
engagement with grief and loss

Teacher guidance on what a poster is, how to prepare and interpret it, and how to use it with visuals
A suitable classroom environment for presenting the prepared posters

Communication and presentation skills

citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Three-level taxonomy of pupils' environmental education: Active, Fragmentary, and Passive
description: Based on the criteria, the article distinguishes three levels of environmental education. "Active" pupils seek environmental knowledge, defend plants and animals, and treat nature "as a goal rather than the means of environmental activities". Fragmentary pupils follow rules of behaviour in nature but rarely take initiative and act only when defence involves no conflict. Passive pupils comply only under adult control, do nothing to prevent ill-treatment of natural objects, and regard nature pragmatically as a means to their goals.

constraints: Levels were identified among senior pupils in the Kazan experimental schools

article_title: The Effectiveness of WhatsApp Mobile Learning Activities Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Knowledge Management
citation: Chokri Barhoumi. (2015). The Effectiveness of WhatsApp Mobile Learning Activities Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Knowledge Management. Contemporary Educational Technology, 6(3), 221-238. https://cedtech.net
title: Activity theory as a three-level framework for analyzing factors influencing participation in mobile-mediated online learning communities
description: The article uses activity theory as the guiding framework to design and analyze interactions in a WhatsApp-mediated learning community. It states that "Activity theory is a framework that researchers use to design and analyze interactions between members of a group and discover factors influencing their participation in online discussion." The framework operates at three levels printed in Figure 1: the technological level (tools, habits, usability), the individual level (subjects and perceived affordances), and the community level (social presence, rules, division of labor), building on Engeström's extension adding community sharing of the same object.
requirements: An activity system with subjects, tools, community, rules, and division of labor, so that participation factors can be examined at each of the three levels
constraints: The article applies the framework to a single blended course context and to factors influencing online discussion participation
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and sharing through collaborative online discussion
examples: The researcher used the framework to interpret the achievement and attitude differences by examining usability and habits, perceived affordances, and social presence, roles, and rules

title: ACE teaching cycle-based experimental calculus curriculum on limits
description: An experimental curriculum modeled on the ACE (Activity, Classroom Discussion, Exercise) teaching cycle, designed to initiate reflective abstraction on the concept of limit. Each day's lesson included reflective activities done in cooperative groups, an instructor debriefing discussion, and individual exercise sets. It covered the same topics, time, and textbook sections as the traditional curriculum, with identical limit examples and the same homework assignments; the stated differences were the collaborative activities and the teacher scripted interactions.

constraints: Evaluated only against a matched traditional section at one midwestern community college

examples: Both curricula were field tested for content validity and approved by an expert panel of teaching-award recipient professors

It applies Engeström's extension, in which "the subject the relations of which to the community are mediatized by rules and the division of labor," organized into six principles (subject, object orientedness, tools, community, division of labor, rules) and three levels: technological, individual, and community.

construction and sharing of knowledge
achievement in a course on computers in instruction

citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Active means of training for the formation of learners' interest in physics
description: The article proposes five active means of physics training: physics in nature, physics in everyday life, physics in technics, physics in science, and history of physics. Each means connects the content of educational material to phenomena or achievements outside the lesson, for example "the explanation of various natural phenomena from the point of physics view" or "examples of various scientific achievements, where knowledge of physics have been used". These means, together with active learning methods, are the components of the developed technique for forming learners' interest in physics.

target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: formation of learners' interest in physics and motivation to study physics

title: Active learning methods for the formation of learners' interest in physics
description: The article selects six active methods for teaching physics according to their influence on the development of learners' thinking: heuristic conversation, creation of problematic situations, home experiments, excursions, solving crosswords, and conducting physics dictations. For example, creation of problematic situations introduces learners to activity during which they are faced with facts that contradict their experience, and home experiments let learners reproduce fundamental physics experiments so that they will feel themselves "discoverers". These methods form the second component of the developed technique.
requirements: Home experiments require safety rules, simple equipment, curiosity, accessibility, and integration in the curriculum
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics

citation: Sahail M. Asassfeh. (2013). Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p85
title: Acuairning: language acquisition and learning as points on a single continuum
description: The article introduces 'acuairning', a blend of acquisition and learning, as a conceptual term placing natural acquisition and formal learning on one continuum rather than treating them as dichotomous. It proposes conceptualizing the learner's experience as depending on "the type, richness, intensity, naturalness, and meaningfulness of input" rather than on the geographical EFL/ESL setting. On this view, teachers can move learners from hyper-heightened consciousness associated with formal learning toward less-heightened consciousness, aligning with communicative language teaching principles, and the difference between implicit and explicit CF becomes less significant.
requirements: The learner must receive sufficient, adequate, comprehensible input for the EFL/ESL distinction to lose value
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal inviting reconceptualization, not as an empirically tested model
target_learners: EFL learners, especially those whose exposure to English is limited to the classroom context
target_learning_goals: Grammatical accuracy in EFL writing
Balancing fluency and accuracy in language learning
examples: The author argues the native/non-native distinction is tied to competence versus performance and that intuitive knowledge is constructed through interaction rather than inherent

peer review skills

description: Because traditional physics teaching gives students the impression that logic matters for physics while hardly showing that creativity is a necessary part of doing physics, the authors argue attitudes are hard to change later. constraints: Students extensively exposed to traditional methods find their attitudes difficult to change in one or two semesters of university education

article_title: A Comparative Study of English Language Teaching Practices at the Access Program and Public Schools
citation: Iqbal, M., & Rafi, M. S. (2018). A Comparative Study of English Language Teaching Practices at the Access Program and Public Schools. Bulletin of Education and Research, 40(3), 231-249. https://pu.edu.pk/journals/index.php/ber/
title: Access classroom practices: activity-based, technology-supported English teaching without examination pressure
description: The Access classroom combines multimedia-rich facilities (multimedia, computer, CDs, white board, UPS) with activity-based teaching and continuous rather than high-stakes assessment. Teachers "teach English language through; showing movies, role plays, group work, peer work, songs, video and board games etc. which are not common in Pakistani public schools." Teachers and students may rearrange the classroom to their needs, and both are free of pass-fail examination pressure, which the article contrasts with the chalk-and-talk, Grammar Translation Method of public schools.
requirements: Modern teaching gadgets (multimedia, computer, CDs, white board, UPS), teachers trained by local and American trainers, and absence of pass-fail examinations with continuous assessment instead
constraints: The article describes this pattern as operating in the after-school Access setting; these practices are reported as not common in Pakistani public schools

target_learning_goals: Development of English linguistic competence and performance across listening, speaking, reading and writing
examples: Access teachers were trained by local trainers and by American trainers in Pakistan and in the United States, and used movies, role plays, group and peer work, songs and games

description: An Excel-based Activity Reporting System with three components — a Daily Log, an Activity Log, and a Case Notes Log — allowed the coach to "maintain electronic case notes and logs and to track the number, type, and duration of coaching contacts and activities." citation: Razfar, A. (2011). Action Research in Urban Schools: Empowerment, Transformation, and Challenges. Teacher Education Quarterly, 38(4), 25-44. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ949874
title: Action research as a critical, collaborative, ground-up paradigm for teacher empowerment and transformation
description: The article defines action research as systematic inquiry conducted by teachers to understand and improve their own school contexts, drawing on Freire's critical pedagogy. It frames action research as a 'critical' tool for empowering educators and underserved communities to define and analyze their own social problems, develop new understandings, and act. Change is assumed to come from the ground up rather than top-down, and inquiry must be a collaborative partnership with colleagues at the school. The article further draws on Cooper and Gause's concept of 'collaborative activism' as the essence of transformative leadership.
requirements: Teachers must be active in a K-12 educational setting where they develop and implement an action plan appropriate for that context
Inquiry must be a collaborative partnership with other colleagues at the school
constraints: The paradigm was developed and applied in the context of a master's program at a Hispanic-serving liberal arts college serving urban educators
target_learning_goals: Developing critical inquiry skills
Fostering teacher empowerment and transformative practice
Building collaborative partnerships

article_title: Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing.
citation: Huang Yue, Jia Jin, Zhan Jun, Li Bo, Gu Qiong, Li Zhengyu. (2024). Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05936-8
title: Use accessible, low-cost animal-tissue models to give trainees realistic surgical practice before operating on patients
description: The article argues that because commercial simulators are costly and "their application limited due to high cost and low-grade simulation", while "Animal models can highly mimic human tissues, and their cost is much lower", choosing an appropriate animal model creates a real-life experience that helps trainees practice surgical skills before performing them on patients. Pre-processing to make the tissue safe and usable
Supervision by trainers during incision, repair and suturing steps

No hemorrhage simulation
Short shelf life of fresh tissue

title: Small-group actor simulation with structured reflective debriefing for communication skills
description: The course pattern places simulations in small groups with a professional actor and a clinical teacher: "The simulation involves a small group of six to ten students, an actor, and a clinical teacher." After each simulation, a reflective debriefing facilitated by the clinical teacher proceeds from the student doctor's perspective, then the actor's, then the whole group, enabling participation, observation, feedback, and reflection.
requirements: A trained improvising actor portraying the patient
A clinical teacher facilitating the debriefing
A small group of six to ten students
constraints: Some students found long feedback discussions uncomfortable and views on time allocation between simulations and feedback varied
target_learning_goals: doctor-patient communication
handling challenging encounters
breaking bad news
examples: Scenarios included shared decision-making, unmotivated patients, patient fears, medical errors, and breaking bad news

title: ACE-C continuous performance task (CPT) for group-administered sustained attention assessment in classrooms
description: The Adaptive Cognitive Evaluation Classroom (ACE-C) battery includes a CPT adapted from the Test of Variables of Attention for iPad administration in group school settings. Participants "press a button with the index finger on their dominant hand when the symbol appeared at the top of the screen (target) and to withhold responses when it appeared at the bottom". It has a 'sustained' condition with targets on 33.3% of trials and an 'impulsive' condition with targets on 66.6% of trials, and yields RT, RTV and d-prime per condition. Adaptive algorithms with a psychometric staircase allow repeated assessment without floor or ceiling effects.

article_title: Breakfast and Exercise Improve Academic and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents.
citation: Kawabata Masato, Lee Kerry, Choo Hui-Cheng, Burns Stephen F. (2021). Breakfast and Exercise Improve Academic and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents. Nutrients 13(4). https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13041278
title: Acute physiological mechanisms account for short-term cognitive benefits of breakfast and exercise
description: The article frames the observed improvements as arising from acute rather than long-term effects: satiation and hunger alleviation, improved fuel and nutrient provision for the central nervous system, and increased synthesis or levels of brain neurotransmitters for breakfast; and exercise-induced catecholamine increases that speed processing, plus possible BDNF-mediated neuroplasticity. The authors state the single-morning intervention "affirms previous literature that some of the improvement elicited from breakfast and exercise is from the acute effects rather than long-term changes in nutritional status or physical fitness".
requirements: Acute intake timing within the morning, since the cognitive reaction-time benefit appeared only at the test-series immediately after the intervention
constraints: The reaction-time improvement did not last until the final test-series, and any BDNF effect may have been limited because the exercise was of moderate rather than higher intensity
target_learning_goals: attention, processing speed, and academic task performance
examples: The authors postulate cocoa flavonols in the Milo drink and hazelnut spread may have contributed to acute cognitive improvements, though this is speculative without a non-cocoa control breakfast

title: Academic tenacity as a multifaceted construct combining grit, resilience, strengths-use, self-control, well-being and growth mind-set
description: Academic tenacity is defined in the article as "the combination of grit, resilience, strengths-use, self-control, psychological well-being and a growth mind-set that provides students with the capacity to thrive at university." The article argues these constructs are strongly interrelated and that measuring one or two alone is overly simplistic. The BUSS operationalises this construct in a single 12-item scale so institutions can take a targeted approach to improving achievement.
requirements: Measurement should cover all six constituent characteristics rather than one or two factors alone
constraints: The authors' contention that academic tenacity outperforms competing measures such as grit alone is untested; they state "Further research is needed to test this assertion"
Developed at a single institution; the authors state it needs to be tested in other universities and in different countries
target_learning_goals: identifying at-risk students for peer mentoring and support services
cultivating academic tenacity through targeted interventions
examples: The BUSS items were drawn from the Grit Scale, Self-Control Scale, CD-RISC 10, Mindset Quiz and WEMWBS, with two strengths-use items generated deductively from a literature review
key_sources: Kannangara Chathurika Sewwandi, Allen Rosie Elizabeth, Carson Jerome Francis, Khan Samia Zahraa Noor, Waugh Gill, Kandadi Kondal Reddy. (2020). Onwards and upwards: The development, piloting and validation of a new measure of academic tenacity- The Bolton Uni-Stride Scale (BUSS). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235157

article_title: Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence.
citation: Sander Paul, de la Fuente Jesús. (2020). Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(15). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155567
title: Academic Behavioural Confidence (ABC) Scale, Spanish-validated version
description: The Academic Behavioural Confidence scale is a 24-item self-report instrument for university students. The article describes it as "a psychometric measure of the confidence of undergraduate students in their anticipated study-related behaviours in a largely lecture-based course". Prior work established "a four-factor model (confidence in attaining grades, studying, attending classes and discussing course material) with adequate reliability and validity". In this study the Spanish-validated version was completed online by Spanish undergraduates, and its four-subscale structure was re-validated by confirmatory factor analysis with item 24 deleted.
requirements: Students respond to the stem "How confident are you that you will be able to..." on a five-point scale from "not at all confident" to "very confident", with higher scores indicating greater confidence in self-efficacious study skills or behaviours.
constraints: Item 24, attend tutorials, "was largely not applicable to those Spanish students" and was deleted for the confirmatory analysis.
The reduced two-item attendance scale's alpha of 0.625 "seems poor", which the authors attribute to the small number of items.
target_learners: undergraduate students in largely lecture-based university courses
target_learning_goals: confidence in anticipated study-related behaviours: attaining grades, studying, attending classes and discussing course material
examples: In this study the scale was completed in Spanish via an online platform by Psychology, Primary Education and Educational Psychology undergraduates at two Spanish universities.
key_sources: Sander Paul, de la Fuente Jesús. (2020). Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(15). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155567

article_title: Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning.
citation: Wijnia, L. & Servant-Miklos, V. F. C. (2019). Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 915–929. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09923-3
title: Achievement goal theory's 2×2 framework: mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals
description: Achievement goal theory (AGT), developed from work on mastery goals (developing competence) and performance goals (outperforming others), was refined by Elliot (1999) and Pintrich (2000) into a performance-approach/performance-avoidance distinction that was empirically validated. Elliot and McGregor (2001) extended the approach/avoidance distinction to mastery goals, yielding four goals: "mastery-approach (striving to learn or improve skills), mastery-avoidance (striving to avoid learning failures or skill decline), performance-approach (striving to outperform others or appear talented), and performance-avoidance (striving to avoid doing worse than others or appearing less talented)". The article notes AGT remains marred by unresolved controversies over labels, measures and definitions.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish the goal dimensions; the article notes Hulleman et al. (2010) showed the 'outperforming others' and 'demonstrating ability' dimensions are differently associated with performance outcomes
constraints: AGT lacks clear founding fathers and carries unresolved controversy among its proponents, including the mastery versus multiple goals debate
target_learners: higher-education and medical students in PBL contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals relate to learning outcomes and motivation in PBL
examples: Of the four studies in the meta-analysis that included AGT measures, only two distinguished performance-approach from performance-avoidance goals and only one differentiated mastery-approach from mastery-avoidance goals
key_sources: Wijnia, L. & Servant-Miklos, V. F. C. (2019). Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 915–929. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09923-3

article_title: Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students.
citation: Donkin Rebecca, Askew Elizabeth, Stevenson Hollie. (2019). Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1745-1
title: Achievement goal theory explains how performance-oriented goals and moderate anxiety drive engagement with video feedback and online learning resources
description: The article uses achievement goal theory as its explanatory framework for why the video group engaged more than the control group. Performance-oriented goals, "whereby students want positive affirmation of their proficiency when performing a learning activity which thereby focusses their motivation to achieve", were notable in the video group because the task was assessed by an Instructor. The article also draws on the idea that moderate anxiety is motivating and that the social system of learning, including being scrutinised, engages students in online environments.
requirements: A learning activity where performance is assessed by an expert or Instructor rather than only by peers
Feedback structures that students perceive as consequential for demonstrating proficiency
constraints: The framework is applied interpretively in the discussion rather than tested directly in the study design
The article notes motivation is multi-faceted and likely influenced by many explicit and implicit variables
target_learners: Undergraduate students in performance-assessed practical courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding motivation to engage with formative feedback and online learning resources
examples: The article interprets the video group's higher tutorial attendance and time on task as evidence that the anxiety of being recorded and assessed by an expert promoted participation in voluntary learning activities, while the control group's lower anxiety reduced interest and engagement
key_sources: Donkin Rebecca, Askew Elizabeth, Stevenson Hollie. (2019). Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1745-1

article_title: How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures.
citation: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z
title: Three validated EBM knowledge tests: ACE, Berlin, and Fresno
description: The article evaluates three commonly used EBM knowledge instruments: "the ACE (Assessing Competency in EBM) Tool with binary answering format", the Berlin Questionnaire with multiple-choice format, and the Fresno test with open-ended answers. The ACE is a 15-item Yes/No test scored 0–15 across four domains; the Berlin is a 15-item five-option multiple-choice test scored 0–15 built around clinical scenarios; the Fresno is an 18-item open-ended test scored 0–124 with scenario-based questions rated in four grade categories.
requirements: The Fresno test requires substantially more time for completion than the other two tests.
constraints: The Fresno test examines each of four EBM areas with a single question, which the authors note may be insufficient for a comprehensive knowledge assessment.
target_learning_goals: assessing EBM knowledge: question formulation, literature search, evidence appraisal and application
examples: All three instruments were translated into Croatian and back-translated, with two statements corrected for clarity.
key_sources: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z

article_title: The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls.
citation: Fuhrmann Delia, Schweizer Susanne, Leung Jovita, Griffin Cait, Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2019). The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls. Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1080/17588928.2018.1504762
title: Academic Diligence Task (ADT): a behavioral measure of diligence as time allocated to tedious math versus games
description: The Academic Diligence Task (Galla et al., 2014) models real-world schoolwork choices: in a split-screen interface, participants freely allocate time between "complete simple single-digit arithmetic problems" and playing entertaining games such as Tetris. Math is deliberately simple and boring so diligence is not confounded with math ability. In this study it was used unaltered with adolescent girls, with diligence operationally defined as the percentage of time spent doing math over a 20-minute session.
requirements: Simple, boring arithmetic so that time-on-math reflects diligence rather than math ability
Instructions highlighting the alleged benefits of practicing math, with participants left alone to reduce demand characteristics
constraints: The article notes the ADT could be improved by including temptation and boredom questionnaire items for both math and games, and by assessing math aptitude and attitudes
target_learning_goals: academic diligence: regulating behavior in the service of academic goals despite tempting distractions
examples: In this study, 40 girls completed three blocks choosing between math and games; diligence averaged 84.14% of time on math, and the task showed convergent validity with grit and self-control questionnaires in its original validation
key_sources: Fuhrmann Delia, Schweizer Susanne, Leung Jovita, Griffin Cait, Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2019). The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls. Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1080/17588928.2018.1504762

article_title: Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Puolakanaho, A., Lappalainen, R., Lappalainen, P., Muotka, J. S., Hirvonen, R., Eklund, K. M., Ahonen, T. P. S., & Kiuru, N. (2018). Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-018-0973-8
title: Acceptance and commitment therapy's six core psychological processes as a trans-diagnostic framework for preventive school-based intervention
description: The article frames acceptance and commitment therapy as a third-wave cognitive therapy in which "acceptance and commitment intervention models combine mindfulness and acceptance with behavioral principles and an understanding of personal values." Recent models aim to reinforce six core psychological processes: flexible present-moment attention and mindfulness, perspective-taking on thinking and feeling, clarifying values and goals, acting in line with those values, willingly accepting unwanted feelings while acting consistently with them, and increasing defusion skills — seeing interfering thoughts as thoughts rather than literal truths. Each process is a trainable psychological skill applicable in any life domain, making ACT a trans-diagnostic treatment that the authors argue can serve preventively to alleviate stress and promote well-being such as academic buoyancy.
requirements: Exercises that target each of the six core processes across program modules
Trained coaches for guidance and motivational feedback in supported delivery
constraints: Studies in school settings were rare at the time; most prior evidence came from clinical samples with face-to-face group delivery
target_learners: Adolescents (11–16-year-olds and ninth-graders) in school settings
target_learning_goals: Psychological flexibility
Defusion and acceptance skills
Values clarification and valued action
Mindfulness
examples: Youth COMPASS operationalizes the processes across five modules: Direction For Life (values/goals), Me And My Mind (defusion), Stalking Myself (present-moment acceptance), Me and Myself (self-as-context/self-compassion), and Me and Other People (valued action in social life)
key_sources: Puolakanaho, A., Lappalainen, R., Lappalainen, P., Muotka, J. S., Hirvonen, R., Eklund, K. M., Ahonen, T. P. S., & Kiuru, N. (2018). Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-018-0973-8

article_title: A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi.
citation: Bvumbwe, T.M. & Mtshali, N.G., 2018, 'A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi', Curationis 41(1), a1766. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v41i1.1766
title: Implement nursing education transformation through formal academic–practice partnerships
description: The model advocates formal, structured strategic relationships between educational and clinical practice settings spanning practice, education and research. The article states that "Academic practice partnership is an important mechanism to strengthen nursing education, practice and research and help nurses become well positioned to lead change and advance health." Figure 1 shows all strategies should be implemented through a collaborative approach, with mutual and shared goals and resource sharing.
requirements: Well-defined strategic relationships between educational and clinical practice settings
constraints: The article ties success of transformation strategies to implementation within this formal collaboration
target_learners: nursing students transitioning between theory blocks and clinical practice
target_learning_goals: narrowing the theory–practice gap and preparing practice-ready graduates
examples: Participants reported that mutual collaboration among academic and practice staff lets them share expertise and build each other's capacity

article_title: Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school.
citation: Hornstra, Lisette; Majoor, Marieke; Peetsma, Thea. (2017). Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 606-629. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12167
title: Multiple goal perspective: three latent achievement goal profiles and their transitions in upper elementary school
description: The study applies the multiple goal perspective, which "posits that certain combinations of achievement goals are more favourable than others in terms of educational outcomes". Using latent profile analysis in two domains, three profiles were identified: an "approach‐oriented" profile with relatively high mastery and performance-approach goals and low performance-avoidance goals; a "moderate/indifferent" profile with average scores on each goal; and a "multiple goals" profile with relatively high avoidance goals alongside high mastery and performance-approach goals. Profile membership was mostly stable (78.12% in language, 85.22% in mathematics).
requirements: Measurement of mastery, performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals per domain (Goal Orientation Questionnaire) so profiles can be derived with latent profile analysis
constraints: The study used a trichotomous goal framework and did not include mastery-avoidance goals, arguing younger students rarely adopt them
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and effort in language and mathematics
examples: Latent profile analyses in Mplus 6.1 across three waves yielded a 3-profile solution for both mathematics and language
key_sources: Hornstra, Lisette; Majoor, Marieke; Peetsma, Thea. (2017). Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 606-629. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12167

article_title: Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model.
citation: Williams, S. N., Thakore, B. K., & McGee, R. (2017). Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-01-0021
title: Academy for Future Science Faculty coaching program
description: The Academy for Future Science Faculty is "a novel coaching program aiming to positively influence biomedical science PhD students' persistence into academic careers, with a particular focus on encouraging and supporting URM students." Cohort 1 recruited 99 students entering PhD programs in Fall 2011, of whom 51 self-identified as URMs, subdivided into 10 coaching groups of 10 students each with faculty coaches from different institutions. The intervention combined annual 2- or 3-day in-person meetings in Chicago with between-meeting videoconferences and email, covering career planning, professional development, and diversity topics. Coaches received diversity training informed by social science theory.
requirements: Faculty coaches selected for track record of mentoring URM scientists
Diversity training for coaches including social science theories and building a community of support
Students and coaches from different institutions to provide an outside voice
constraints: The program was not designed to substitute for social communities of graduate school research groups and departments
Recruiters were unable to recruit more URM coaches (including Black/African-American, Hispanic male, or Native American coaches) for this cohort
target_learners: Early-stage URM biomedical PhD students in the United States interested in academic careers
target_learning_goals: Career planning and professional development
Persistence into academic careers
Coping with isolation, discrimination, and microaggressions
examples: Students completed individual development plans and self-assessment documents discussed in coaching groups
Sample meeting topics included "Stereotypes, Assumptions, Bias, Difference, Diversity, Discrimination: Realities of Biomedical Research Communities"

article_title: Distributed practice. The more the merrier? A randomised bronchoscopy simulation study.
citation: Bjerrum Anne Sofie, Eika Berit, Charles Peder, Hilberg Ole. (2016). Distributed practice. The more the merrier? A randomised bronchoscopy simulation study. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.30517
title: Accutouch high-fidelity virtual reality bronchoscopy simulator (CAE Healthcare)
description: The training and assessment platform used in the study: "an Accutouch high-fidelity virtual reality simulator from CAE Healthcare®, Quebec, Canada." It consists of a proxy flexible bronchoscope, a robotic interface device, a computer with simulation software, and a monitor. The virtual patient responds to trainee instrumentation with coughing, and the simulator provides force-feedback which enhances realism. It supplies metrics including procedure time, wall collisions, time in red-out, and percent-segments-entered.
requirements: An instructor introduction, an airways atlas, and a 15-min instruction video available on the simulator preceded training
constraints: Testing was done without simulator utilities or the atlas, and simulator-measured metrics only; OSATS assessments were deselected due to lack of assessor blinding opportunity and feasibility
target_learning_goals: Flexible bronchoscopy navigation and systematic inspection of the bronchial system to the sub-segmental level
examples: Participants practised unsupervised on the same simulator case three times per session with a 20-minute time limit per case

article_title: Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training.
citation: Sattler David N., McKnight Patrick E., Naney Linda, Mathis Randy. (2015). Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130450
title: Anchoring bias from academic grading habits distorts grant rating scale use
description: The article proposes that reviewers, accustomed to academic grading where scores below the 60th percentile all receive the same fail grade, may inappropriately apply that model to grant scales. On the NIH 9-point scale, a score in the 55% range represents a "good" proposal whereas 0% to 11% represents a "poor" proposal; a reviewer intending a poor score near the 50th percentile would inflate it to mid-scale, producing restriction of range and inaccurate scoring. The training video teaches this bias explicitly.
requirements: Reviewers must be taught that grant scale percentages do not have equivalent meaning to academic grading percentages
constraints: The article states it did not examine all cognitive biases that may affect the selection of scale values, as doing so was beyond the scope of the study
target_learners: Grant peer reviewers transitioning from academic grading contexts
target_learning_goals: Accurate use of the full range of grant rating scales
examples: The video gave the example that a 50-percent-range score typically means failing in academia but mid-range on the NIH scale means a good proposal.
key_sources: Sattler David N., McKnight Patrick E., Naney Linda, Mathis Randy. (2015). Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130450

article_title: Understanding the challenges to facilitating active learning in the resident conferences: a qualitative study of internal medicine faculty and resident perspectives.
citation: Sawatsky Adam P., Zickmund Susan L., Berlacher Kathryn, Lesky Dan, Granieri Rosanne. (2015). Understanding the challenges to facilitating active learning in the resident conferences: a qualitative study of internal medicine faculty and resident perspectives. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v20.27289
title: ACTIVE teaching format for resident noon conferences
description: A structured conference format the authors built from this study's results to give faculty a way to facilitate active learning with minimal faculty development time and effort. "This ACTIVE format was centered on 3–5 focused learning points, clinical questions, small group break-out discussions, and frequent summarization." It is presented as one example of an easily implemented alternative to comprehensive lecturing.
requirements: Faculty development or guidelines and training for faculty unfamiliar with facilitating active learning.
constraints: The article notes structured formats like problem-based and team-based learning require large programmatic change and may not fully suit the residency environment; the ACTIVE format is offered as one example needing further work.
target_learning_goals: resident interaction and engagement
medical knowledge achievement
examples: The authors report using this study's results to build the format, described in a cited prospective controlled study of the ACTIVE format versus standard lecture.

article_title: Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine.
citation: Ilic Dragan, Nordin Rusli Bin, Glasziou Paul, Tilson Julie K, Villanueva Elmer. (2014). Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-114
title: ACE tool: a 15-item dichotomous assessment of EBM competency across steps 1-4
description: The ACE tool presents users with a patient scenario, a search strategy and a hypothetical article extract, then asks 15 yes/no questions covering question formulation, literature searching, critical appraisal and application of evidence. Items 1-11 assess knowledge and skills, while items 12-15 assess attitudes toward implementing EBM in clinical practice. The authors state it "provides a novel assessment that measures user performance across the four main steps of EBM" and is the first such instrument with a dichotomous outcome measure.
requirements: Requires a patient scenario, search strategy and article extract; scoring is one point per correct answer to a maximum of 15
constraints: In its current form, with only one patient scenario, search strategy and article, it does not necessarily permit repeated use on the same cohort; it assesses only steps 1-4, not the evaluation step
target_learners: medical trainees at novice, intermediate and advanced EBM levels
target_learning_goals: evidence based medicine competency: asking answerable questions, searching, critical appraisal, applying evidence
examples: 342 Monash medical trainees completed the tool online with a 60-minute limit; mean completion time was 12.8 minutes
key_sources: Ilic Dragan, Nordin Rusli Bin, Glasziou Paul, Tilson Julie K, Villanueva Elmer. (2014). Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-114

article_title: Can training in advanced clinical skills in obstetrics, neonatal care and leadership, of non-physician clinicians in Malawi impact on clinical services improvements (the ETATMBA project): a process evaluation.
citation: Ellard David R, Chimwaza Wanangwa, Davies David, O'Hare Joseph Paul, Kamwendo Francis, Quenby Siobhan, Griffiths Frances, on behalf of The ETATMBA Study Group. (2014). Can training in advanced clinical skills in obstetrics, neonatal care and leadership, of non-physician clinicians in Malawi impact on clinical services improvements (the ETATMBA project): a process evaluation. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2014-005751
title: Accredit professional training for non-physician clinicians to raise its status and quality
description: During development and delivery of the ETATMBA training, the authors found that accreditation mattered for how the programme was received: "it became clear that raising the status and quality of the educational experience through accreditation was a vital strategy." NPCs in Malawi are described as often undervalued with no clear career pathways, so formal accreditation is presented as a way of legitimising and strengthening their educational experience. The principle applies to designing up-skilling programmes for cadres of health workers who lack established professional recognition.
requirements: A credentialing body or partner (in this case Malawian institutions) able to accredit the training programme
constraints: The article states this as a strategy learned during programme establishment in Malawi, not a tested manipulation
target_learners: Non-physician clinicians and other undervalued mid-level health worker cadres
target_learning_goals: Professional development and advanced clinical skills recognition
examples: After ETATMBA, the accredited approach was extended to a further 60 NPCs in obstetrics and five other specialties with Malawi Ministry of Health support
